To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the constitutive production of carbon monoxide is increased in the pancreatic islets of the ob/ob diabetic mouse and that this islet production of carbon monoxides contributes to their hyperinsulinemia.

carbon monoxide (a gas produced from heme by the enzyme heme oxygenase) is produced in the islets of Langerhans at a rate of 1 nmol.min(-1).mg protein(-1) and that this gas acts as an important regulator of insulin release and as a messenger coordinating the rhythmicity of insulin release in the islets.

(1) the islets from ob ob mice have a sixfold higher rate of CO production than the islets from the lean controls; (2) the increased CO production contributes to the hypersecretion of insulin from the ob/ob islets; and (3) CO acts as a synchronizer of Ca2+ signals in the beta-cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of pulsatility in the beta-cell and the role of the endocrine islet as an integrated functional unit.
the mechanisms of pulsating insulin release and the coordination of the beta-cell activity in the islet.
the role of CO as a neurotransmitter with a dual effect on the islet function, namely, a positive modulator and a synchronizing messenger of the rhythmic insulin release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CO is a positive modulator and synchronizer of the beta-cell rhythmycity.
CO and NO are both important regulators of the pulsatile insulin secretion, but that they act in opposite directions.
CO, in concert with NO, is a key regulator of insulin release.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CO is an islet hormone with a dual role: it stimulates insulin secretion and it synchronizes the activity of the islet beta-cells.
CO and NO, both of them with a stimulatory action on cGMP, are involved in the synchronization of [Ca2+](i) oscillations and the pulsatile release of insulin.

CO is an important modulator of islet function and that the increased production of CO in ob/ob islets may have important implications for the development of the diabetic phenotype in the ob/ ob mouse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the islets of ob/ob mice are characterized by an increased generation of CO, and that this islet hyperproduction of CO contributes to a hyperinsulinemia.

the islets in ob/ob and lean mice differ in the rate of production of CO, but not in the rate of NO production, and that the CO production is a key factor in the regulation of pulsatile insulin secretion.
CO, in addition to serving as positive modulator of the glucose-stimulation of insulin release, acts as a messenger coordinating the Ca2+ signals within and among the pancreatic beta-cells.
